 Judgment

This criminal appeal is preferred by the appellant under Section 29 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, calling in question the legality, correctness and propriety of the order dated 18-03-2021 passed by the MMTC-V, Bengaluru, on I.A. No.1 in Crl. Misc. No.40/2021,
whereby the trial court has (i) directed deletion of Respondent No.2 from the array of parties, and (ii) declined to exercise interim jurisdiction under Section 23(2) of the Act in relation to protection against alienation,
return of Stridhan, monetary relief and educational expenses of the hearing-impaired minor child.

22. In light of the rival contentions, the following pivotal points emerge for determination in this appeal:
1) Whether the trial court was justified in deleting Respondent No.2 from the proceedings and in refusing to exercise interim jurisdiction under Section 23(2) of the PWDV Act despite specific allegations of physical and economic abuse?
2) What order?
23.

This Court, while exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 29 of the Act, is duty- bound not only to scrutinize the correctness of the order on facts, but also to examine whether the learned Magistrate has exercised jurisdiction in consonance with the constitutional mandate,
statutory scheme and binding judicial precedent governing the field.
25. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, is not an ordinary procedural statute.

entities.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: It is a welfare legislation having deep constitutional roots in Articles 14, 15(3) and 21 of the Constitution of India.
Article 15(3) authorizes special protection to women, while Article 21 guarantees a life of dignity, shelter, safety and economic security.

26. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vimlaben Ajitbhai Patel v. Vatslaben Ashokbhai Patel, (2008) 4 SCC 649, has held that:
"Economic security and right to shelter are integral facets of the right to life under Article 21."

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
27. Therefore, any judicial approach that mechanically excludes a woman from statutory protection under the Act must be tested against the constitutional obligation of the Courts to protect dignity,
shelter and livelihood of women.

The foundational error committed by the trial court lies in the deletion of Respondent No.2 on the premise that there is no shared household and that she is a female relative.

This reasoning stands directly overruled by the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in: Hiral P. Harsora v.
Kusum Narottamdas Harsora, (2016) 10 SCC 165, wherein the expression "adult male" in Section 2(q) was struck down and it was held that:
"Any relative of the husband, whether male or female, can be proceeded against under the Act if domestic violence is alleged."

Hiral P. Harsora v.
Kusum Narottamdas Harsora, (2016) 10 SCC 165
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 29. Thus, after Hiral Harsora, sisters-in-law are fully amenable to jurisdiction under the Act.

This position has been repeatedly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in: Smt. Renuka v.
Smt. Saroja, 2019 SCC OnLine Kar 1796, where it is held that:
"Deletion of female relatives at the threshold is impermissible when allegations disclose active participation in domestic violence."

sentences.text: 30. In the present case, the appellant has made specific, categorical and direct allegations against Respondent No.2 of physical assault, instigation, and collusion in depriving her economic rights.
At the interim stage under Section 23, the Court is not expected to weigh evidence with finality, but only to examine whether a prima facie case exists.
The deletion of Respondent No.2 without trial amounts to pre-judging the allegations and extinguishing statutory remedies at the threshold, which is legally impermissible.
31. The trial court gravely erred in holding that the restraint against alienation is "purely civil in nature".

This finding reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of Section 3(iv) of the Act, which defines "economic abuse" to include:
"alienation of assets whether movable or immovable in which the aggrieved person has an interest or is entitled to use by virtue of the domestic relationship".
32.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in V.D. Bhanot v. Savita Bhanot, (2012) 3 SCC 183, clearly held that:
"Deprivation of proprietary and residential rights constitutes one of the most serious forms of domestic violence."

 "Economic abuse includes systematic  deprivation of financial and proprietary entitlements and cannot be reduced to mere non-payment of maintenance."

sentences.text: 35. In the present case, the appellant has pleaded that: a) She invested money in the construction of the property; b) The rental income is enjoyed by Respondent No.1; c) The alienation is in favour of Respondent No.2; d) The transfer is intended to defeat her residential rights.
Thus, the act complained of is not a neutral civil transaction, but a weaponized economic act intended to domestically dis-empower the aggrieved woman, which squarely falls within Section 3(iv).
The trial court's refusal to intervene therefore amounts to abdication of jurisdiction.
36. The rigid insistence by the trial court on the continued existence of a shared household is also legally unsustainable.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in:Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja, (2021) 1 SCC 414, clarified that:
"A shared household is not confined to a house where the husband and wife lived together last, but includes any household where the aggrieved woman lived in domestic relationship."

opennyai_summary.facts:
This criminal appeal is preferred by the appellant under Section 29 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, calling in question the legality, correctness and propriety of the order dated 18-03-2021 passed by the MMTC-V, Bengaluru, on I.A. No.1 in Crl. Misc. No.40/2021,
whereby the trial court has (i) directed deletion of Respondent No.2 from the array of parties, and (ii) declined to exercise interim jurisdiction under Section 23(2) of the Act in relation to protection against alienation,
return of Stridhan, monetary relief and educational expenses of the hearing-impaired minor child.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The said Order is total miscarriage of Justice and no reasonable man can come to this conclusion of deleting the Respondent from array of Respondent.
b) The trial court has committed an error in passing an Order and direction to the office of the Court to delete the Respondent no.2 from the array of Respondent and further direction not to issue Notice to Respondent No.2.
The conclusion made by the trial court that there is no Domestic Relationship between the Appellant and Respondent No.2 as the Appellant and Respondent No. 1 were staying separately and not in the shared household along with Respondent No.2.
The trial court has failed to understand the main role played by the Respondent no.2 along with Respondent No.1 by inflicting physical, verbal emotional and Economic abuse to the Appellant.
Alienating an immovable asset to defeat the right of victim wife under the said Act constitutes Domestic Violence; coming interalia of the ambit of definition of "Economic abuse".
Respondent No.1 has executed an Agreement of Sale with Respondent No.2 to defraud the Appellant.
Respondent no.1 is trying to dispose of house hold effects such as the alienation of assets of immovable property in which Appellant has an interest or is entitled to use by virtue of Domestic relationship.
The said act of Respondent No.1 is covered under the definition of "Economic Abuse "under S. 3 (iv) of the Act.
The trial Court has failed to understand and pass the protection order prohibiting the Respondent No.1 to further Sale the Schedule Property to Respondent No.2.Also Respondent No.2 is covered under the definition of "Respondent "as contemplated under Section 2(q) of the Act as Appellant is in Domestic Relationship with Respondent No.2 who is the elder Sister of Respondent No. 1.; against who the Appellant as Aggrieved person has sought relief under the Act.
Appellant is entitled for her Stridhan and all her gold jewellery purchased by her own earnings as mentioned in the Schedule-2 of the Application.
The trial court has committed an error in not considering the documents and evidence produced by the Appellant.
g) The Impugned order is totally biased and lacks proper application of facts and laws.
The trial court has considered and decided the case and application on the basis of several illegalities.
The Impugned Order is an error and it is also arbitrary and unreasonable and hence may be set aside by this Appellate Court.
h) The trial Judge was not liberal in interpreting the Definition of Respondent as contemplated under S.2 of the Act.
The findings of trial court is opposed to the evidence and probabilities of the case as such it is liable to be set aside by this trial court.
I) The impugned order is not sustainable in law and illegal footings and it is also opposed to probabilities of the case.
This Court, while exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 29 of the Act, is duty- bound not only to scrutinize the correctness of the order on facts, but also to examine whether the learned Magistrate has exercised jurisdiction in consonance with the constitutional mandate,
statutory scheme and binding judicial precedent governing the field.
25. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, is not an ordinary procedural statute.
It is a welfare legislation having deep constitutional roots in Articles 14, 15(3) and 21 of the Constitution of India.
Article 15(3) authorizes special protection to women, while Article 21 guarantees a life of dignity, shelter, safety and economic security.
The deletion of Respondent No.2 without trial amounts to pre-judging the allegations and extinguishing statutory remedies at the threshold, which is legally impermissible.

Thus, the act complained of is not a neutral civil transaction, but a weaponized economic act intended to domestically dis-empower the aggrieved woman, which squarely falls within Section 3(iv).
The trial court's refusal to intervene therefore amounts to abdication of jurisdiction.
Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in Smt. Manjula v. Ramesh, ILR 2021 KAR 3254, has further held that interim orders on Stridhana cannot be mechanically refused.
Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shalu Ojha v. Prashant Ojha, (2019) 7 SCC 200, has held that:
